title: From Dubai Boardroom to Death Zone: Shradha Gupta's Audacious Everest Campaign
excerpt: The DBS Bank executive and Indian mountaineer is attempting the world's highest peak barely eight months after her historic Manaslu summit, compressing a decade's climbing arc into three years
body:
When Shradha Gupta stood on the summit of Mount Manaslu at 8:06 am on September 26, 2025, she crossed a line that separates serious trekkers from genuine high-altitude mountaineers. Eight months later, she is on the slopes of Everest, attempting to summit the world's highest peak at 8,848 metres — a progression that typically takes experienced climbers the better part of a decade.

## The Manaslu Foundation

Manaslu, the world's eighth-highest mountain at 8,163 metres, sits firmly within the 'death zone' — altitudes above 8,000 metres where supplemental oxygen becomes not a luxury but a survival necessity. Gupta summited as part of Nirmal Purja's Elite Exped team, roping alongside elite guide Tenji Sherpa, and the successful ascent established her firmly among India's emerging generation of endurance mountaineers.

What makes the achievement more remarkable is its context. Gupta took up high-altitude climbing only after the COVID-19 pandemic, redirecting a passion for recreational hiking into something far more ambitious while based in the UAE. Within three years, she had summited three of the Seven Summits — Kilimanjaro, Elbrus, and Aconcagua — completed the Everest Base Camp trek, and then graduated directly to an 8,000-metre peak.

## The Everest Attempt

The 2026 Everest spring season is one of the most crowded on record. Nepal has issued 492 climbing permits — a record — generating $8.3 million in royalties alone. The season has also been one of the most tragic, with five climbers dying in the Himalayas by mid-May, including a Sherpa guide in the notoriously dangerous Khumbu Icefall.

Gupta's expedition is navigating these conditions alongside hundreds of other climbers from around the world. The summit window — a narrow 3-7 day period in mid-May when the jet stream weakens enough to allow ascent — requires precise timing and acclimatisation that leaves zero margin for error at temperatures of -32°C and wind gusts of 46 km/h.

The outcome of her attempt has not been confirmed at the time of reporting.

## A Dual Identity That Resonates

By day, Gupta leads Corporate Business for the Middle East at DBS Bank, one of Asia's largest lenders. The dual identity — finance executive during the week, death-zone mountaineer during expedition windows — has drawn attention both within the climbing community and among working professionals, particularly in the Indian diaspora.

For NRIs in the Gulf, Gupta's story carries particular weight. The UAE hosts one of the world's largest Indian expatriate communities, estimated at over 3.5 million, and her trajectory from Dubai-based banker to 8,000-metre summiter mirrors a broader pattern of diaspora Indians pursuing extreme endurance goals alongside demanding careers. From marathon runners in London to ultra-cyclists in Silicon Valley, the Indian professional abroad is increasingly redefining what a 'side pursuit' can look like.

## The Bigger Picture

If Gupta summits Everest, it would mark her second 8,000-metre peak and position her for an even more ambitious high-altitude programme — potentially joining the small club of Indian women who have stood on top of the world. The first Indian woman to summit Everest, Bachendri Pal, did so in 1984. Since then, the list has grown steadily, but the combination of a post-pandemic start and corporate career makes Gupta's path distinct.

The climbing world will watch closely. Not because the mountain cares about your backstory — Everest is famously indifferent to ambition — but because the speed of Gupta's progression raises genuine questions about how structured training, elite expedition support, and sheer determination can compress timelines that were once considered fixed.

Whatever the outcome, Gupta has already demonstrated something that resonates far beyond base camp: that the gap between 'I could never do that' and a summit bid is smaller than most people think, and wider than anyone who hasn't been above 8,000 metres can fully appreciate.
